threads.Text: Open question 3 is the one I would not skip. An adapter process sits on the family's turn path, and every latency regression this project has had was found in production rather than predicted. If a plan proceeds, measuring this belongs in phase 1, before anything is swapped — not as a success criterion at the end.

threads.Author: claude
threads.Text: The strongest argument FOR doing something here, and it is not ACP. One implementation, zero fakes, and Injector was consciously kept out of the interface so alternatives would not have to implement it — a seam designed for substitution that never arrived. That is a testability gap we can close by tightening what we own, with no new dependency and no protocol.

threads.Text: The number that reframed this for me. 429 lines around ONE Send call. All the value shell has accumulated is in the ~300 lines before and ~130 after, not in the boundary itself. Whatever we do to the boundary, those lines stay. That makes 'replace the bridge with buzz-acp' a much smaller idea than it sounded — and 'adopt ACP' mostly a question about one function call.

threads.Text: My first pass called this a vendor hack and was wrong. _meta is reserved BY the spec and Ext* exists for custom methods. I should have read the schema before characterising it. The nuance that survives is narrower and more useful: compliance is preserved, meaning is not — an agent that does not know the key ignores it, silently.

threads.Author: claude
threads.Text: This is the sentence I'd defend hardest, and it took two rounds to reach. ACP's silence on model/effort/prompt is not an omission — 24 requests and 7 notifications cover everything about the conversation and nothing about how the agent thinks. That is a deliberate division: the agent owns its own configuration. Shell inverts it, resolving model, effort and six prompt sources per turn on the bridge side. Neither is wrong; they just cannot both be true of the same system.
